History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
- 28-year-old woman* with a first episode of 3-day persistent, severe right-predominant headache with photophobia and transient visual “shooting lights”; clinician suspects migraine and arranged in-person neurological examination and stronger analgesia.  
(*Age not explicitly stated; adult female per context.)

History:
- Presenting complaint: “Blinding” headache for 3 days.
- Onset/Duration: Sudden onset on waking 3 days ago; continuous since.
- Location/Character: Diffuse but worst over right eye; constant pressure/stabbing, rated 8/10, ↓ to 5/10 with ibuprofen (does not fully resolve).
- Exacerbating factors: Bright light, sudden standing or head movement.
- Relieving factors: Partial relief with ibuprofen; able to sleep (headache does not wake her).
- Associated symptoms:
  • Photophobia.  
  • Visual disturbance – brief “shooting lights.”  
  • Mild nausea; no vomiting.  
- Pertinent negatives: No focal neurologic deficits (numbness, weakness, speech), no fever, neck stiffness, sinus/URTI symptoms, cough, epistaxis, weight change.
- Impact: Unable to focus on work; missed 1–1.5 workdays (works from home).

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.  
- Childhood “pain” episode (resolved; no diagnosis).

Medications:
- Combined oral contraceptive pill (brand unspecified) – dose/route/frequency not documented; started 1 year ago.  
- Ibuprofen PRN for headache – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
- No known drug, food, or environmental allergies.

Social History:
- Lives alone; works from home.  
- Smoking: Never.  
- Alcohol: ~3 drinks once weekly.  
- Recreational drugs: Denies.  
- No recent travel.

Family History:
- Mother suffers from migraine with vomiting.  
- No other familial conditions disclosed.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.  
- General / Neurologic / Fundoscopic / Cardiovascular / ENT: Not examined (video consult).

Investigations:
- None to date.  
- Plan for in-person neurological exam with fundoscopy and blood pressure measurement.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
Acute severe headache most consistent with first-episode migraine with visual aura; however secondary causes (e.g., CVST) must be excluded given estrogen OCP use and positional features.

DDx Integration:
1. Migraine with visual aura – photophobia, visual phenomena, unilateral severe pain, family history; no red-flag neuro signs.  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – risk factor (combined OCP), new persistent headache, mild positional worsening; no neuro deficits (needs exclusion).  
3. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension – young woman with visual symptoms; but headache worse standing (opposes) and no papilledema yet.

Issue 1: Acute severe headache
- Arrange urgent face-to-face appointment for full neurologic examination and fundoscopy.  
- Safety-net: if headache intensifies, changes character, or new neuro symptoms occur, attend Emergency Department immediately.

Issue 2: Symptom control / analgesia
- Prescribe stronger NSAID (name and dose not specified in transcript) to take with food.  
- May take paracetamol concurrently (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
- Continue current ibuprofen only if additional NSAID not taken (per standard practice).

Issue 3: Hormonal contraception and migraine risk
- Re-check blood pressure at upcoming visit.  
- If migraines with aura confirmed, discuss switching from combined OCP to non-estrogen method.

General plan items
- Review after physical examination to reassess diagnosis and management.  
- Provide patient with contact details for support line for appointment booking and interim advice.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No vitals or physical findings recorded; medication doses/frequencies undocumented; patient age not explicitly stated.  
● Transcript vs DDx conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor audio gaps but core clinical data intact.
